chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ali ibn Ma'bad, from Wasil ibn Sulayman, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I heard him saying: 'God commands and does not will, and wills and does not command.'
He commanded Iblis to prostrate to Adam, and willed that he not prostrate — and had He willed, he would have prostrated.
And He forbade Adam from eating from the tree, and willed that he eat from it — and had He not willed, he would not have eaten.

key_terms.أَمَرَ: amara — to command; refers to the legislative/religious command (amr tashri'i), what God enjoins as duty
key_terms.شَاءَ: sha'a — to will/desire; refers to God's ontological/creative will (irada takwiniyya), what God decrees to occur in the world
key_terms.نَهَى: naha — to forbid; God's prohibition of eating from the tree
key_terms.يَسْجُدَ: yasjuda — to prostrate (sajda); the commanded act of worship toward Adam as a mark of honor

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between God's command and God's will in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches a fundamental distinction in Islamic theology between God's legislative command (amr) and His ontological will (masha'a). This hadith, narrated through a reliable chain of five transmitters to Abdullah ibn Sinan, illustrates the doctrine with two Quranic episodes: Iblis was commanded to prostrate but God willed he would refuse (so the divine plan for testing mankind was fulfilled), while Adam was prohibited from the tree yet God willed he would eat (so the plan of descent and vicegerency on earth would unfold). This teaching was crucial for Shia theological understanding of free will, divine determinism, and the distinction between religious obligation and cosmic decree.
